payload.claim: The problem statement is explicit and twofold: "Add `saffron/gates/core/constant_mutants.py` with one public function, `constant_mutants(diff, acceptance, patterns, test_paths)`" and separately, of this file, "Rewrite two docstrings in `saffron/gates/core/witness.py` and change no code there." The diff does neither: no `saffron/gates/core/constant_mutants.py` exists anywhere in the tree (confirmed by a direct glob), and `saffron/gates/core/witness.py` gained roughly 150 lines of new code — `CLAIM_TEMPLATE` (line 320), `_new_side` (326), `_overlaps_added` (361), `_readable_files` (366), `_candidate_constants` (374), `_witness_name` (397), `_witness_text` (405), `_names_whole_word` (419) and `constant_mutants` (423) itself — plus three new imports (`re`, four names from `saffron.gates.core.integrity`, `matches` from `saffron.gates.core.scope`, and `WitnessPatterns` from `saffron.repos.policy`). Every acceptance-criterion witness still passes because the tests import `constant_mutants` from `saffron.gates.core.witness` rather than from the module the spec names, so no test catches the relocation. Functionally the suite wiring in `saffron/gates/suite.py` is unaffected either way, but the spec drew the module boundary deliberately (keeping `witness.py`'s own role untouched beyond its two docstrings, with the new diff-reading logic isolated in its own file), and that boundary was not honored. A person should decide whether this warrants a follow-up to split the module as specified.
